## In 60 seconds

A mapping system stores the chamber as a **triangle mesh**: vertices, edges and triangular faces, with activation
times and voltages attached to the vertices. Three operations on that mesh come back again and again. The
**gradient** on each triangle turns activation times into a conduction-velocity vector, and it is exact for a planar
wave. The **Laplace–Beltrami operator**, the Laplacian on a curved surface, drives smoothing, interpolation and
simulation; its standard discretization weights each edge by the cotangents of the two angles opposite it, and those
weights turn negative on badly shaped triangles. **Geodesic distance**, the shortest path that stays on the surface,
is needed for "how far from this point" questions; adding up edge lengths along the mesh overestimates it by up to
15% however fine the mesh is, while methods that solve a differential equation on the surface converge. The mesh is
part of the measurement.

## From the field

- **Velocity needs both density and accurate timing.** Sparse, unevenly spaced and uncertain data make conduction
  velocity hard to compute, and many methods exist [@cantwell2015]. In lab part B, 1 ms of timing noise gives a
  median speed error of 47% at 1-mm spacing and 9% at 8-mm spacing: closer points need better timing, not less.
- **Open tools work on the mesh.** OpenEP provides functions for chamber geometry, activation mapping and
  conduction-velocity mapping on exported data; its area and volume were correlated with those of the clinical
  platform [@williams2021]. The face areas in this module (@eq-m06-gradient) are the same building block.
- **Shortest paths along edges are biased.** On a regular triangle lattice, the edge path is longer than the straight
  line by up to $2/\sqrt3$, 15.5%, at every resolution (demo m06-d1). Fast marching on triangulated domains
  [@kimmel1998] and the heat method [@crane2012] compute distances that converge as the mesh is refined.
- **Triangle shape matters.** Slivers and obtuse angles give negative cotangent weights (demo m06-d2), which can make
  smoothing produce values outside the range of the data. In lab part C, a strongly jittered flat patch has 58 of
  its 1121 edges with negative weights.

## Derivations

**Symbols used throughout.** $V$, $E$, $F$ numbers of vertices, edges and faces; $g$ genus (number of handles). $u_i$
a value at vertex $i$; $T$ local activation time (ms). $A_f$ area of face $f$; $\mathbf N_f$ its unit normal;
$\mathbf e_i$ the edge of a face opposite vertex $i$, oriented counterclockwise about $\mathbf N_f$. $\mathbf v$
conduction-velocity vector (mm/ms = m/s). $\alpha_{ij}$, $\beta_{ij}$ the two angles opposite edge $ij$; $A_i$ the
area assigned to vertex $i$ (one third of each incident face); $L_C$ the cotangent matrix, $\mathbf A$ the diagonal
matrix of $A_i$. $\Delta$ the Laplace–Beltrami operator; $\lambda$, $\phi$ an eigenvalue and eigenfunction; $R$
sphere radius; $l$ degree. $t$ diffusion time, $h$ mean edge length, $\boldsymbol\delta_s$ a unit value at the source.

### Meshes

A closed mesh that is topologically a sphere obeys Euler's formula; every closed triangle mesh also shares each edge
between two faces:

$$
\chi = V - E + F = 2 - 2g, \qquad 2E = 3F
$$ {#eq-m06-euler}

So a closed chamber surface without holes has $\chi = 2$ and about twice as many faces as vertices. Cutting a hole,
for example at a valve or vein opening, adds a boundary loop and lowers $\chi$ by one; a single flat patch, a disk,
has $\chi = 1$. A test that $\chi$ is what you expect catches duplicated vertices, cracks and flipped faces before any
map is computed. Lab part A builds subdivided icosahedra (icospheres): 12 vertices with five neighbors and every other
vertex with six.

**Key takeaways**

- $V - E + F$ is a cheap check of mesh topology; a closed surface without handles gives 2.
- A closed triangle mesh has about twice as many faces as vertices.

### Gradients and conduction velocity

Values at the three vertices of a face define one linear function on it. Its gradient lies in the plane of the face:

$$
\nabla u\big|_f = \frac{1}{2A_f}\sum_{i \in f} u_i\,(\mathbf N_f \times \mathbf e_i), \qquad \mathbf v = \frac{\nabla T}{\lvert\nabla T\rvert^2}
$$ {#eq-m06-gradient}

Each term rotates the opposite edge by 90° in the plane, and its length over $2A_f$ is one over the triangle's height.
For activation times $T$, the wavefront moves along $\nabla T$ at speed $1/\lvert\nabla T\rvert$, which gives
$\mathbf v$. The formula reproduces any linear function exactly, on any triangle shape, so a planar wave gives the
exact speed and direction (lab part B). Its error comes from the data: a timing error $\delta T$ over a triangle of
height $h_i$ changes the gradient by about $\delta T/h_i$, so small triangles amplify timing noise. m25 compares the
velocity methods built on this formula with fitting methods [@cantwell2015].

**Key takeaways**

- The per-face gradient is exact for linear data; its error comes from timing error divided by triangle size.
- Conduction velocity is $\nabla T/\lvert\nabla T\rvert^2$, in mm/ms (= m/s) when distances are in mm.

### The Laplace–Beltrami operator

On a surface, the Laplacian of $u$ is the divergence of its surface gradient. The standard discretization is the
**cotangent formula** [@pinkall1993]:

$$
(\Delta u)_i \approx \frac{1}{A_i}\sum_{j \in \mathcal N(i)} \frac{\cot\alpha_{ij} + \cot\beta_{ij}}{2}\,(u_j - u_i)
$$ {#eq-m06-cotan}

where $\mathcal N(i)$ is the set of neighbors of $i$. It follows from the energy $\tfrac12\int\lvert\nabla u\rvert^2$ of
the piecewise-linear function: the derivative of that energy with respect to $u_i$ is minus the sum. The edge weights
depend only on angles. On a flat mesh the formula
maps every linear function to zero at interior vertices, and on a regular equilateral lattice it gives exactly 4 for
$x^2 + y^2$ (lab part C). On the unit sphere $\Delta z = -2z$: the typical (median) error falls about fourfold per
refinement, from $1.4\times10^{-2}$ to $2.2\times10^{-4}$ over three levels, but the worst error, at the 12 vertices
with five neighbors, stays near 0.25 with these vertex areas. Errors concentrate where the mesh is irregular.

The weight of an edge is negative when its two opposite angles add up to more than 180°, that is, when the edge is
not **locally Delaunay**. Negative weights break the property that a smoothed value lies between its neighbors.

::: {.demo #m06-d2 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m06-d2-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m06-d2"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m06-d2-cotan-weights.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: the weight $(\cot\alpha + \cot\beta)/2$ of one interior edge shared by two triangles (@eq-m06-cotan), with
  the triangles drawn on a common edge. Tested against `epml.meshes.edge_cotan_weight`.
- Parameters: the two opposite angles, 20–160° each; free choices for illustration.
- What it ignores: the rest of the mesh, vertex areas and boundaries.
:::

The Laplacian's eigenfunctions are the surface's natural vibration modes. On a sphere they are the spherical
harmonics:

$$
-\Delta \phi = \lambda\,\phi, \qquad \lambda_l = \frac{l(l+1)}{R^2}\ \ (l = 0, 1, 2, \dots,\ \text{multiplicity } 2l + 1), \qquad -L_C\,\boldsymbol\phi = \lambda\,\mathbf A\,\boldsymbol\phi
$$ {#eq-m06-spectrum}

The last form is the mesh version, a generalized eigenproblem with the sparse matrices $L_C$ and $\mathbf A$. On a
level-4 icosphere (2562 vertices), the first eigenvalues on the unit sphere come out as 0, 2 (three times), 5.991
(five times) and about 11.96 (seven times) (lab part D). Low modes describe smooth shape and smooth maps; the graph
neural networks of m39 also mix values over mesh neighbors.

**Key takeaways**

- The cotangent Laplacian uses only angles and areas; it is exact for linear data on flat meshes.
- Its weights turn negative on non-Delaunay edges, and its error concentrates at irregular vertices.
- Its eigenvalues converge to the surface's; on a sphere they are $l(l+1)/R^2$.

### Distances on a surface

The geodesic distance $\phi$ from a source solves the eikonal equation $\lvert\nabla\phi\rvert = 1$ with $\phi = 0$ at
the source; m42 uses the same equation with a speed ([eq-m42-eikonal](m42-physics-informed-ml.qmd#eq-m42-eikonal)).
The simplest estimate is the shortest path along mesh edges (Dijkstra's algorithm). On an equilateral lattice, the
shortest edge path in direction $\theta$ from a lattice direction is longer than the straight line by the factor
$(\sin\theta + \sin(60^\circ - \theta))/\sin 60^\circ$, largest, $2/\sqrt3 \approx 1.155$, at 30°. The factor does
not depend on the edge length, so refining the mesh does not remove it.

::: {.demo #m06-d1 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m06-d1-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m06-d1"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m06-d1-edge-paths.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: the shortest path along the edges of an infinite equilateral triangle lattice compared with the straight
  line, for a direction you choose. The ratio is a closed form, checked against Dijkstra on a 41 × 41 lattice in
  `tests/test_m06_meshes.py`.
- Parameters: direction 0–120°; the ratio repeats every 60°.
- What it ignores: irregular meshes and curvature; on real meshes the bias varies from point to point.
:::

Methods that treat the mesh as a surface converge instead. Fast marching extends a front from the source in order of
arrival and handles triangulated domains in $O(M\log M)$ steps for $M$ points [@sethian1996; @kimmel1998]. The
**heat method** solves two sparse linear systems [@crane2012]:

$$
(\mathbf A - t\,L_C)\,\mathbf u = \boldsymbol\delta_s, \qquad \mathbf X = -\frac{\nabla u}{\lvert\nabla u\rvert}, \qquad L_C\,\boldsymbol\phi = \nabla\!\cdot\mathbf X
$$ {#eq-m06-geodesic}

Heat diffused for a short time $t$ from the source points away from it, so its normalized gradient gives the
direction in which distance grows; the last step finds the function whose gradient best matches that direction. The
authors use $t = h^2$ [@crane2012]. On the unit sphere, the edge-path error stays near 0.19 at every refinement,
while the heat method's mean error falls from 0.045 at level 2 to 0.0086 at level 5 (lab part E).

**Key takeaways**

- Edge paths overestimate distance by up to 15.5% on a regular lattice, at any resolution.
- Fast marching and the heat method solve the eikonal equation on the surface and converge.

## Clinical correlate

::: {.callout-note title="Pending clinical review"}
This section describes published findings only. It is not guidance for patient care, and it has
not yet been reviewed by an EP physician.
:::

**Where this shows up in EP.** Conduction velocity is computed from activation times recorded at scattered points on
the chamber surface, and a survey of the methods describes how sparse, unevenly spaced and uncertain data make this
hard [@cantwell2015]. OpenEP, an open data format and analysis platform for exported mapping data, provides functions
for geometry, activation and conduction-velocity mapping on the chamber mesh; its surface area and volume were
correlated with the clinical platform's, and when the authors investigated a systematic bias between the two, OpenEP
recovered accurate values better than the clinical platform [@williams2021]. Every one of these numbers depends on the mesh and the operators in this module.

**What the evidence is.** A methods survey [@cantwell2015], a software validation study on clinical mapping data
[@williams2021], and the numerical-methods literature [@pinkall1993; @kimmel1998; @crane2012].

**What a reader should ask:**

- **How was the velocity computed?** Per-triangle gradients, fits or another method; and how timing error was
  handled (@eq-m06-gradient).
- **How fine and how regular is the mesh?** Thin triangles amplify timing error and give negative Laplacian
  weights (@eq-m06-cotan).
- **How were distances measured?** Along edges or by a geodesic method (@eq-m06-geodesic).

## How experts think

Before trusting a map computed on a mesh, ask:

1. **Is the mesh what it claims to be?** Count $V - E + F$ and boundaries (@eq-m06-euler).
2. **How big are the triangles compared with the timing error?** Velocity error scales as timing error over triangle
   height (@eq-m06-gradient).
3. **Are the triangles well shaped?** Obtuse and sliver triangles give negative weights (@eq-m06-cotan).
4. **Which distance is used?** Edge paths are biased; geodesic methods converge (@eq-m06-geodesic).
5. **Does the result change when the mesh is refined or remeshed?** If it does, the mesh is part of the answer.

One sentence to keep: **every map computed on a mesh inherits the mesh's resolution, regularity and topology.**

## Cheat sheet

| Quantity | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Euler (@eq-m06-euler) | $V - E + F = 2 - 2g$; closed triangle mesh: $2E = 3F$, $F \approx 2V$ |
| Gradient (@eq-m06-gradient) | exact for linear data; velocity $\nabla T/\lvert\nabla T\rvert^2$, speed $1/\lvert\nabla T\rvert$ |
| Cotangent Laplacian (@eq-m06-cotan) | edge weight $(\cot\alpha + \cot\beta)/2$, negative if $\alpha + \beta > 180°$ |
| Spectrum (@eq-m06-spectrum) | sphere: $l(l+1)/R^2$, multiplicity $2l+1$; mesh: $-L_C\phi = \lambda\mathbf A\phi$ |
| Edge paths | regular lattice: up to $2/\sqrt3$ (15.5%) too long at any resolution |
| Heat method (@eq-m06-geodesic) | heat, normalize, Poisson; $t = h^2$ |

**Values used in this module**

| Value | Source |
| --- | --- |
| Fast marching on triangulated domains in $O(M\log M)$ steps | @kimmel1998 |
| Heat-method time step $t = h^2$ | @crane2012 |
| Speed errors with timing noise, Laplacian and eigenvalue errors, path ratios, heat-method errors | our own code |

## Interview questions

Try each question before you open its model answer. In a real interview, say which assumptions you
are making.

**Q1. A closed mesh has 1000 vertices and 2990 edges. Is something wrong?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Probably. A closed triangle mesh without handles has $2E = 3F$ and $V - E + F = 2$, so $E = 3(V - 2) = 2994$. A
smaller count suggests boundaries, holes or non-manifold edges (@eq-m06-euler).

</details>

**Q2. How do you compute the gradient of activation time on one triangle?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Treat $T$ as linear on the face: sum each vertex time times the opposite edge rotated 90° in the plane, divided by
twice the area (@eq-m06-gradient).

</details>

**Q3. Why is conduction velocity $\nabla T/\lvert\nabla T\rvert^2$ and not $\nabla T$?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

$\lvert\nabla T\rvert$ is time per distance, the slowness; speed is its inverse. Dividing $\nabla T$ by its squared
length keeps the direction and gives length $1/\lvert\nabla T\rvert$ (@eq-m06-gradient).

</details>

**Q4. Points 1 mm apart with 1 ms of timing error. What happens to velocity?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The gradient error is about 1 ms/mm, as large as the gradient of a 1 m/s wave itself, so speed can be badly wrong; in
lab part B (0.8 m/s, 1-mm spacing) the median error is 47%. Wider triangles or better timing are needed (@eq-m06-gradient) [@cantwell2015].

</details>

**Q5. Write the cotangent Laplacian.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

$(\Delta u)_i \approx \frac{1}{A_i}\sum_j \frac{\cot\alpha_{ij} + \cot\beta_{ij}}{2}(u_j - u_i)$, with $\alpha$ and
$\beta$ the angles opposite edge $ij$ (@eq-m06-cotan) [@pinkall1993].

</details>

**Q6. When is a cotangent weight negative, and why does it matter?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

When the two opposite angles add up to more than 180°, so the edge is not locally Delaunay. Smoothing can then push
values outside their neighbors' range (@eq-m06-cotan; demo m06-d2).

</details>

**Q7. Your Laplacian is accurate almost everywhere but bad at a few vertices. Where would you look?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

At irregular vertices, such as those with five or seven neighbors, and at poorly shaped triangles; on the icosphere
the worst error sits at the 12 five-neighbor vertices (@eq-m06-cotan; lab part C).

</details>

**Q8. What are the Laplace–Beltrami eigenvalues of a sphere of radius 10 mm?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

$l(l+1)/100$ mm⁻²: 0, 0.02 (three modes), 0.06 (five modes) and so on (@eq-m06-spectrum).

</details>

**Q9. Why not compute surface distance with Dijkstra on the mesh edges?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Paths are forced along edges, so they are too long, by up to $2/\sqrt3$ on a regular lattice, and the bias does not
shrink with refinement (demo m06-d1).

</details>

**Q10. Describe the heat method in three steps.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Diffuse heat from the source for a short time; normalize the negative gradient to unit length; solve a Poisson
equation whose solution has that gradient (@eq-m06-geodesic) [@crane2012].

</details>

**Q11. What does the time step $t$ do in the heat method?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

It sets how far the heat spreads before its direction is read. The authors use $t = h^2$ [@crane2012]. In our code,
on a level-4 unit sphere, $t = 0.1h^2$ more than doubles the mean error (0.030 against 0.013); the end of the
lab suggests trying $t = 10h^2$.

</details>

**Q12. Two teams compute velocity maps from the same data and disagree. What would you compare?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Mesh resolution and quality, the velocity method (per-triangle or fitted), timing preprocessing, and how outliers
were removed (@eq-m06-gradient) [@cantwell2015].

</details>

## Self-check

Short checks you can do in your head. Open each answer after you have tried it.

**S1. A closed mesh without handles has 5120 faces. How many vertices?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$E = 7680$, so $V = 2 + E - F = 2562$ (@eq-m06-euler).

</details>

**S2. Activation time increases by 2 ms per mm. Speed?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

0.5 mm/ms = 0.5 m/s (@eq-m06-gradient).

</details>

**S3. Both angles opposite an edge are 60°. Its weight?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$\cot 60^\circ = 1/\sqrt3$, so the weight is $1/\sqrt3 \approx 0.58$ (@eq-m06-cotan).

</details>

**S4. Opposite angles 120° and 70°. Sign of the weight?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

Negative: they add up to more than 180° (@eq-m06-cotan).

</details>

**S5. How many independent modes has the sphere at eigenvalue $6/R^2$?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

Five ($l = 2$, $2l + 1 = 5$) (@eq-m06-spectrum).

</details>

**S6. On an equilateral lattice, in which direction are edge paths most biased?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

At 30° from a lattice direction, by $2/\sqrt3$ (demo m06-d1).

</details>

## Literature figures

These figures are worth looking at alongside this module. We link to them instead of copying them:
some licenses do not allow reuse here, and others we could not confirm. Each entry says what to
look for and where this module explains it.

- **Geodesics in heat.** Crane and colleagues show the three steps of the heat method on surface meshes and compare
  it with fast marching [@crane2012]. This module: distances on a surface.
- **Geodesic paths on triangulated surfaces.** Kimmel and Sethian show distance maps and shortest paths computed by
  fast marching on triangulated domains [@kimmel1998]. This module: distances on a surface.
- **Conduction-velocity methods.** Cantwell and colleagues illustrate triangulation and fitting methods on mapping
  data [@cantwell2015]. This module: gradients and conduction velocity.

## Further reading

- **Discrete operators.** The cotangent formula [@pinkall1993].
- **Distances.** Fast marching [@sethian1996; @kimmel1998]; the heat method [@crane2012].
- **Mapping data.** Velocity methods [@cantwell2015]; the OpenEP platform [@williams2021].
